problem: The sentence lists CMP and TST among instructions that update flags "only if they have the S suffix". CMP, CMN, TST and TEQ have no separate non-flag form: they always update the flags, and the S bit is implied in their encoding. A student may look for a "CMPS" instruction that does not exist.
fix: Data-processing instructions such as ADD, SUB and AND update N, Z, C and V only when the S suffix is present (ADDS, SUBS, ANDS). The compare and test instructions CMP, CMN, TST and TEQ always update the flags and have no non-flag form.

problem: "R0-R3 pass the first four arguments and return values" can be read as four return values. Also R0-R3 are scratch, so a callee may destroy them.
fix: R0-R3 pass the first four arguments; the return value comes back in R0 (R0 and R1 for a 64-bit value). A callee may overwrite all of R0-R3, so the caller must save them if needed.

problem: "R4-R11 hold local variables" is not exact under the standard ARM calling convention: R9 is a platform register that a given platform may reserve, and R12 is the scratch register (IP) that linker veneers may destroy.
fix: R4-R8, R10 and R11 hold local variables and must be preserved by the callee. R9 is platform-specific: some platforms reserve it. R12 is the scratch register IP and need not be preserved across a call.

problem: The note on PC says "next instruction", but Section 2 states that a read of R15 gives the current instruction's address plus 8 in ARM state. "Next instruction" suggests current + 4 and contradicts the rule just taught.
fix: Label the PC note "address of instruction being fetched: current + 8 (ARM), current + 4 (Thumb)".

problem: "Thumb uses 2-byte instructions and an offset of 4" is only true of classic 16-bit Thumb. Thumb-2 also has 32-bit instructions, yet a read of R15 still returns current + 4, so the reasoning by instruction size misleads.
fix: The Thumb pipeline is one stage shallower, so a read of R15 returns current + 4. This holds for 16-bit and 32-bit Thumb-2 instructions alike; the "2-byte instruction" picture is only a memory aid.

problem: The lead says every ARM program uses the sixteen registers and "the CPSR", and names a Cortex-M motor controller. Cortex-M cores expose xPSR plus PRIMASK, FAULTMASK and BASEPRI, with no ARM/Thumb state bit and no User/FIQ/IRQ/Supervisor mode encoding of the classic kind.
fix: Add one clause: on classic ARM cores (ARM7, ARM9, ARM11, Cortex-A and Cortex-R at this level) the status register is the CPSR as described here; Cortex-M cores use the xPSR and separate mask registers, covered later.
